system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}
user:
CONCEPT: Track structure Monte Carlo
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Covers event-by-event transport versus the condensed-history approach, the physical, physicochemical and chemical stages, and the role of cross-sections (dielectric formalism, phase effects, uncertainties). Also covers how direct and indirect damage are scored into strand breaks and clustered damage. Excludes the general Monte Carlo dosimetry method for clinical dose calculation.

ATOMS:
- MED-PATH-C08-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: Track structure Monte Carlo codes simulate particle transport event by event, tracking the individual physical interactions, in order to reach the nanometric spatial resolution needed to link radiation track structure to biological effects.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PATH-p0232-s72] However, in order to simulate the physics at the nanoscale and to possibly link it to the biological effects of radiation with track structure properties in the nm regime [54], an event-by-event tracking of the different physical events is necessary to allow for better spatial resolution.
    [MED-PATH-p0232-s73] Therefore, so-called track structure codes have been developed for applications in micro- and mostly nanodosimetry.
- MED-PATH-C08-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: Track structure is the nanometric-scale spatial distribution of all energy deposits (energy transfers) produced by the primary radiation and its secondary particles, notably electrons.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PATH-p0229-s71] Indeed, in this context, it is necessary to “zoom in” on the scale of the target’s constituents at the nanometric scale to look at all the energy deposits (or energy transfers) produced by the initial radiation, as well as the secondary particles, notably the electrons.
    [MED-PATH-p0229-s72] This is the study of the so-called track structure of radiation.
- MED-PATH-C08-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: Track structure codes must include cross sections for ionization, electronic excitations below the ionization threshold and, ideally, vibrational or rotational excitations of the medium, in principle for all interacting particles but particularly for secondary electrons.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PATH-p0232-s74] Indeed, in order to model all the physical interactions taking place in the physical stage, these codes need to include cross sections for simulating ionization, electronic excitations below the ionization threshold, and, ideally, vibrational or rotational excitations of the medium, in principle for all the interacting particles but particularly for secondary electrons, for the reasons explained in Sect. 4.3.2.
- MED-PATH-C08-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: Most theoretical models for the cross sections used in track structure codes are based on the first Born approximation using the dielectric formalism, in which the Energy Loss Function of the material characterizes inelastic interactions with charged particles and allows calculation of the mean free path and inelastic cross sections.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PATH-p0232-s81] Nevertheless, most of the theoretical models for the calculation of the cross sections used in these codes are based on the first Born approximation that uses the dielectric formalism.
    [MED-PATH-p0232-s82] Here, the properties of a given material in terms of characterizing the inelastic interactions with charged particles are given in what is called the Energy Loss Function (ELF).
    [MED-PATH-p0232-s83] This function allows calculating the mean free path and thus the inelastic cross sections.
- MED-PATH-C08-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: Direct strand breaks are scored from energy deposits in DNA volumes, for example using an energy threshold of often 17.5 eV in the nucleotide backbone, or, in the PARTRAC code, a uniform-probability linear function from 5 to 37.5 eV.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PATH-p0234-s73] From the resulting energy deposition values or interactions registered in the DNA volumes, direct damages are calculated using different approaches depending on the TS code.
    [MED-PATH-p0234-s74] For instance, in some cases, an energy threshold value (often of 17.5 eV) in the nucleotide backbone is used to define a direct strand break [30, 80].
    [MED-PATH-p0234-s75] Others, as in the case of the PARTRAC code, use a uniform probability linear function from 5 to 37.5 eV [81] in order to calculate the resulting direct strand breaks, taking into account that very small energy depositions from vibrational excitations can also lead to this kind of DNA damage.
- MED-PATH-C08-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: Because experimental Energy Loss Function data were obtained in the optical limit (zero momentum transfer), the function must be extended to non-zero momentum transfers using dispersion algorithms based on electron gas theory, which redistribute the imaginary part among ionization and excitation levels while keeping their sum consistent with the experimental data.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PATH-p0232-s85] As the existing experimental data have been obtained in the optical limit (i.e., for a zero momentum transfer), it is necessary to extend the calculation of this function for non- zero momentum transfers.
    [MED-PATH-p0232-s86] Different dispersion algorithms based on the electron gas theory [53] are then used to redistribute the imaginary part of the function between the different ionization and excitation levels while preserving the agreement of their sum with the initial experimental data.
- MED-PATH-C08-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: Gas-phase atomic ionization and excitation cross sections, which some track structure codes use, are in principle unsuitable for low-energy excitations of valence electrons in water, because such excitations are sensitive to the electronic structure of the target.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PATH-p0232-s80] However, still, some track structure codes use atomic ionization/electronic excitation cross sections [58] obtained in the gas phase even if, in principle, they are not suitable for low energy excitations of valence electrons in water, since such excitations are sensitive to the electronic structure of the target [54, 59–61].
- MED-PATH-C08-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: Low-energy interaction cross sections depend on the state of the medium as well as its composition, so gas-phase and condensed-phase cross sections differ, and experimental cross sections for biological media in the condensed state are very difficult to obtain, with only a few data under specific conditions existing for liquid water.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PATH-p0232-s76] An important point to consider is that at these low energies, the interaction cross sections depend on the composition of the material but also on its state.
    [MED-PATH-p0232-s77] That is to say that the cross sections are not the same for a medium in a gaseous or a solid state.
    [MED-PATH-p0232-s78] This leads to a particular difficulty because it is very difficult (not to say, almost impossible) to obtain experimental cross sections for biological media in their condensed state [24].
    [MED-PATH-p0232-s79] Only a few data obtained under very specific conditions exist for liquid water [56, 57] and these data are the basis for the set of models utilized to calculate the cross sections used by most track structure codes.
- MED-PATH-C08-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: Condensed-history Monte Carlo, which groups many scattering events into fewer artificial steps much longer than the particle mean free path with continuous energy loss, is used for dosimetry and most microdosimetry of very energetic particles but lacks the nanoscale resolution that event-by-event track structure simulation provides.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PATH-p0232-s70] As we described earlier in this chapter, particle transport through matter using MC codes is generally handled via a “condensed history” (CH) approach [53], currently used for dosimetry and the majority of microdosimetry applications for very energetic particles.
    [MED-PATH-p0232-s71] In such a CH approach, many scattering events are grouped into fewer artificial steps, much longer than the mean free path of the particle, using multiple-scattering theories and a continuous energy loss along those steps.
    [MED-PATH-p0232-s72] However, in order to simulate the physics at the nanoscale and to possibly link it to the biological effects of radiation with track structure properties in the nm regime [54], an event-by-event tracking of the different physical events is necessary to allow for better spatial resolution.
- MED-PATH-C08-S3-04 | S3
  ATOM: Condensed-history Monte Carlo groups many scattering events into fewer artificial steps much longer than the particle mean free path, using multiple-scattering theories and continuous energy loss, so it lacks the nanometric resolution that track structure codes obtain through event-by-event tracking.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PATH-p0232-s71] In such a CH approach, many scattering events are grouped into fewer artificial steps, much longer than the mean free path of the particle, using multiple-scattering theories and a continuous energy loss along those steps.
    [MED-PATH-p0232-s72] However, in order to simulate the physics at the nanoscale and to possibly link it to the biological effects of radiation with track structure properties in the nm regime [54], an event-by-event tracking of the different physical events is necessary to allow for better spatial resolution.
